Dairy Industry Act

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext:
That the Order of the House for the second reading of Bill No. 186, an act to amend The Dairy Industry Act, 1914, be discharged and the said bill withdrawn.
He said:	On the occasion when this bill
was before the House last week I made a fairly full explanation of the reasons why I ask that this motion be carried, and I do not think it calls for any further explanation at this time.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext:
This bill has rather a
checkered history, which I think should be reviewed. The bill was introduced pursuant to a resolution about a week ago. As introduced it provided merely for certain corrections in the Dairy Industry Act of 1914. The corrections were of a minor character, rather numerous in total, but none of them of far-reaching consequence. The minister, on introducing the resolution and carrying it through committee, told the House that there was nothing in the bill respecting oleomargarine at all. He did so in response to a query from the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie):	Nor was there in such bill any
reference to oleomargarine. The subsection which dealt with that subject in the original act of 1914 was left intact. That was the form in which the resolution went through, and the form in which the bill was introduced and was passed on by this House for a second reading. If there is any rule of parliament that is obvious, and that at the same time is vital, it is that when parliament	passes an act, first,
second and third reading, or any stage, the act remains as so passed by parliament, until varied by parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext: Is my right hon. friend not mistaken in saying "second reading"?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext: I said "first." The bill received only a first reading.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext: The right hon. member said "second reading."

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext:
If so, I should have said first. The preceding resolution doubtless received its regular readings. The bill was introduced and read a first time only. Having been read a first time, the bill so read was the bill before the House and that was appointed for second reading, and no other bill. Rule 53 of this House provides that bills when read shall be certified by the
Clerk of the House in order that the terms of the bill so read may be officially stated and officially known. The time for second reading arrived; the Order of the Day was called by the government on Thursday last, and instead of moving the second reading, the minister rose and stated as follows:
Owing to certain changes having been made by parliamentary counsel in the drafting of this bill which while not changing the meaning of the measure, make it more different and more difficult to explain, I mew that the bill be discharged from the order paper with a view of redrafting and resubmisson to the House.
Whereupon I asked the minister:
Will the minister explain how the bill is mo* difficult to explain if the meaning is not changed?
I invite the attention of the House to the minister's repfy. This is an example of vacuous profundity which I do not think has any parallel in the annals of parliament:
As drafted by parliamentary counsel portions of the former bill were inserted that were not in the bill submitted to me.
Does any hon. gentleman know what that means? In the first place, after a bill passes this House a first reading, . parliamentary counsel has nothing to do with it. It is the bill as passed that comes up for second reading. In the next place, what should come up for second reading was all that was in the bill as passed. But the minister says that parliamentary counsel put in the bill something that was in it before and that was not submitted to him. I really do not know what was in the minister's mind and I have sought, though sought in vain, to delve to the bottom of it. He proceeded:
That makes the bill appear quite different from what was contemplated, and the intention of the draftsman and counsel would be more difficult to explain.
Subsequently the minister proceeded to read the bill as printed, for the bill as printed differs wholly from the bill as passed. The bill as printed provided a clause excluding oleomargarine from Canada in the plainest possible terms. I have the bill before me, and it says:
Section 5 of the said act is repealed, and the following is substituted therefor:
This is the new bill:
5. No person shall-(a) manufacture, import into Canada, or offer, sell or have in his possession for sale, any oleomargarine, margarine, butterine, or other substitute for butter, manufactured wholly or in part from any fat other than that of milk or cream.
The minister's explanation of the meaning of this addition, which he says was inserted by parliamentary counsel after the bill was read a first time, is really equally interesting. The minister told the House that the bill
Dairy Industry Act

had been so changed that, as it stood now, it appeared to authorize the manufacture or sale of oleomargarine.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext: That should be "prohibit."

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext: It should have read "prohibit"?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext: I think you will find that is corrected in the revised Hansard.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext:
I will read those words:
Notwithstanding that, however, on the face of it the bill as now drafted appears as if we were authorizing the manufacture or sale of oleomargarine.
The minister now says that he should have said "prohibit."

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext: In the revised Hansard my hon. friend will find it reads that way.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext: On the next page I find the same thing repeated, so the minister duplicated his mistake. Perhaps, as is suggested from behind me, that is on the principle that two negatives would make an affirmative.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext: It does not affect the situation, anyway.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext:
It affects the minister. The minister says at page 3456:
Yet I find another bill on the order paper apparently authorizing the manufacture of oleomargarine.
He used the word "authorized" for "prohibit" twice, in two separate speeches four or five pages apart. I do not know what was wrong with the minister.' I could not understand his explanation then.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext: That is the reason why I wanted a new bill.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext: He made no explanation. He simply either deliberately or otherwise befuddled the House. Why is he withdrawing this bill? What is the object of withdrawing it? The bill before this House is not the printed bill; the bill before this House is the Very bill which the minister introduced. Because something else is printed, that does not make it a bill of this House. I was not aware, when the discussion was on in the first place, of the actual facts. I sought to become aware by listening to the minister, but I made no progress.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext: That is what I thought.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext:
I have learned the facts since. Certainly the minister thought no one

would make progress. No human being would make progress listening to him. He had everything upside down. What I argue is this: The House passed the bill a first reading and this is the bill before the House.
Mr. MACKENZIE-KING: My right hon. friend says that the House passed a bill on the first reading. He says that this is the bill which passed the first reading. I have the bill that passed the first reading with the mark on it. This is not the bill to which my right hon. friend refers.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext: I know that. The Prime Minister does not get my point. Somebody might get up a bill purporting to be a bill up for second reading on the order paper; but no bill can be up for second reading that is not passed by this House on the first reading. It is the government's business to get the bill passed in the House. The bill passed the House exactly as it passed it for first reading. Because this is a bill printed on a sheet and called Bill 186, that does not make it Bill 186. Bill 186 is Bill 186 as it passed this House on its first reading.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext: May I read the clause of the bill as it passed this House on the first reading?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext:
If my right hon. friend will look at the legislation, he will find there are five clauses. Clause 1 there is no question about. Clause 2 in the bill that passed this House on a first reading begins:
Section 5 of the said act is amended by adding at the end of paragraph (b) thereof the words "or less than 80 percentum of milk fat" [DOT], and by striking out in paragraph (c) thereof, in the second line the words "what is generally known as", and in the third line thereof the words "nor add any milk or cream or butter."
That is all there is in the second clause of the bill which passed the first reading in this House. When the second reading was called there appeared on the order paper the bill which I hold in my hand now, section 2 of which reads:
Section 5 of the said act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
5. No person shall-
(a) manufacture, import into Canada, or offer, sell or have in his possession for sale, any oleomargarine, margarine, butterine, or other substitute for butter, manufactured wholly or in part from any fat other than that of milk or cream.
That section was inserted by the law officers of the House after the first bill had gone to them. It was inserted without the knowledge of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), who knew nothing whatever

Oleomargarine
about it and who, as soon as he learned that the clause had been incorporated in the bill, immediately took exception to it and on that ground asked to have the bill withdrawn.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext:
What the Prime Minister has stated, up to his assertion that this clause was inserted without the consent of the Minister of Agriculture, or without his knowledge, is exactly what I said myself. The Prime Minister puts it this way:	He says
that when the bill came up for second reading another bill appeared on the order paper, and he proceeds to quote a clause referring to oleomargarine as section 2 of that bill which repeals section 5 of the act. What I am arguing is that such a bill did not appear on the order paper; what was on the order paper was a motion that Bill 186 should be read the second time. Because another printed bill appeared-not Bill 186 that passed the House, but another bill with an added clause in it- that did not make it Bill 186. Bill 186 is Bill 186 as passed, and consequently that is the government measure yet, the measure they intended to introduce and to have to go through all the stages in this House. Neither parliamentary counsel nor any other officer of the House, with or without the instructions of the minister, can alter a bill as passed by parliament. It is a strange thing to me that parliamentary counsel should do anything of the kind without the authority of the government, or at least the authority of any department of the government. I cannot see how he can, without any authority whatever, add to a bill a clause a hundred times more important than all the rest of the bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext: That is exactly what I have stated-without the authority of any minister of the Crown.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext: Did he have the authority of any officer of the department?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext:
I cannot say
as to that. The ministry is responsible for the measures it introduces.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: THE DAIRY INDUSTRY ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT BILL No. 186 WITHDRAWN
speechtext:
The ministry is responsible for the conduct of its officers, and if any officer of any department or of this House took upon himself to alter the records of the House, then it is the business of the government to bring him to book. I cannot believe that parliamentary counsel would insert a clause of this consequence without any authority at all from the department. It may be that the minister did not directly confer it; but whoever did, if he did it without any authority, it is the duty of the government to get the
explanation which that officer can give. And beyond the question of the responsibility of the government for the conduct of its officers and of the officers of the House, there is this further fact which I would impress upon hon. members again: the bill before parliament now is not the altered bill, because a bill cannot be altered by an officer; it can be altered only by parliament. The bill now before us is the original bill the government introduced. Now, why does the minister withdraw a bill which he introduced and which, in every speech that he has made since, he has stated to be all right?
Resolution (Mr. Motherwell) agreed to: bill withdrawn.

speakerposition: topic
Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I beg to move:
That the notice of motion in the name of Mr. Carroll, respecting a measure to amend the oleomargarine act, have precedence over all other business, except the introduction of bills, questions, and notices of motion for the production of papers, on Wednesday, the 6th June instant.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: * I suppose, Mr. Speaker, that this is the closing scene of the drama; we are now at the stage that the government wished to reach. What is the result of it all? The government is afraid to, or it cannot, bring down a policy with relation to the subject of oleomargarine. One minister smiles in delight over the impo-tency of an administration of which he is a member. This government is going around like one of the birds of the air-I think it is the cuckoo-that lays its eggs in the nests of other birds knowing that those other birds can take care of them, hatch them and i ear the young better than it can itself. This is a cuckoo government. It cannot propound or give birth to any policy on oleomargarine, but it hopes in some way or other to escape governmental responsibility by laying this egg in the nest of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll), trusting that fertility may result. Why cannot the government face the situation? Governments have faced greater difficulties.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
What is
your policy?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Our policy is on the
statute books to-day, where it has been for years. We faced the matter as a government.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
What is your policy now?
Business oj the House

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Let the government
bring down its policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Excise
speechtext: Cuckoo!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What is to be thought
of a member of the government sitting in his seat helpless to propound what should be a government measure, calling upon the opposition to furnish the administration with a policy? The government, in a word, is simply endeavouring to escape the responsibility that rests upon it by seeking if possible to get over a difficulty along some bypath, led by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll).

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Fine!

speechtext: Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE FURTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext:
On a previous occasion
1 promised my right hon. friend (Mr. Meig-hen) that I would submit a statement regarding any legislation which the government intends to bring down before the close of the session.
The Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment (Mr. Beland) has already given notice of a bill to amend the Pension Act arising out of the recommendations of the royal commission that has been investigating the subject of pensions.

There are also to be introduced a bill to amend the Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act and a short amending bill to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment Act arising out of the report of the royal commission on lake grain rates, there will be a bill to amend the Shipping Act, giving the government power by order in council to suspend the coasting laws.
A bill concerning a close season for halibut fishing in Pacific waters.
A bill to amend the Fisheries Act to reduce the fee for salmon cannery licenses.
A bill for further advances to the harbour commissioners of Montreal.
A bill to amend the Biological Board Act.
In connection with the Department of Finance there will be a bill to amend the Income Tax Act and bills respecting the Finance Act and the Audit office respectively.
There will also be a bill respecting the guarantee of railway bonds already authorized.
A bill providing for the three-year branch line construction programme, of which mention has been made by the Minister of Railways and Canals.
A bill to amend the Dry Dock Act of 1910
A bill to amend the Feeding Stuffs Act.
A bill to amend the Dairy and Cold Storage Act.
A bill to amend the Public Archives Act. It is proposed to change the name to the Department of Historical and Public Records.
Possibly there will be other legislation based on the reports of the committees to which have been referred the Bank Act, Redistribution, the Civil Service Act and matters pertaining to agriculture. There will also be Supplementary Estimates.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext: I would suggest the Prime Minister might go back and get another Speech from the Throne.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:
Mr. Speaker, will there be an opportunity for discussion of the matters that are to be placed upon the agenda for the Imperial and Economic conferences?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The government will have occasion to ask for the passing of an estimate to make provision for expenses in connection with these conferences, and at that time I should think there would be ample opportunity to discuss matters pertaining thereto. If not, a time can be specially arranged for the purpose if so desired.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does the Prime Minister propose to state to the House the lines of policy he intends to follow or the specific proposals he will himself advance on the occasion of these conferences?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I shall be glad to answer any questions that may be asked. I happen to have here the latest information the government has received with respect to what is anticipated to be taken up at the proceedings of the Imperial Conference, and I might give it to the House. The despatch requests that the information be given in a general form, and therefore I will only outline the main features.
As in 1921, the opening meeting will include statements as to the general position on the main issues of Imperial policy. The preliminary statement may be followed by a report on foreign affairs since 1921, and by a consideration of the present problems and future policy. A discussion as to naval, military and air defences. A review of the naval situation resulting from the Washington Conference and arrangements for future cooperation in all branches of defence. At some stage of the proceedings attention will be given to the principles referred to it from the Imperial Economic Conference regarding Imperial air and wireless communications. There will probably be certain economic questions of special importance. Australia suggests the discussion of the marriage of women with foreigners. That I think, Mr. 3454	COMMONS
Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
Speaker, by way of an outline of what is anticipated for the coming conference, contains about all the information the government has thus far received.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The Prime Minister stated that he would answer any questions asked him. I would like him to regard my question now placed before him as a request that he do lay before the House a statement of the lines of policy he purposes following on behalf of this Dominion at these conferences and of any proposition he intends to advance himself. I do not mean at the present moment; but that a time be fixed for his doing so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My right hon. friend will appreciate that it is only possible to do that in so far as the government is aware of the questions to come up for discussion at the conferences. I may say broadly that certainly with respect to anything of importance involving expenditures our attitude will be that it must be subject to future ratification by this parliament.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I desire to invite the attention of the committee, Mr. Speaker, to the first resolution to be found on page ii of Votes and Proceedings of Friday, May 11, providing for a 10 per cent discount in regard to goods coming under the preferential tariff when imported direct through our Canadian ports:
1.	Resolved, that the Customs Tariff, 1907, be amended by repealing section five, and substituting therefor the following:
5. That the importer of goods entitled to the benefits of the British Preferential Tariff shall be entitled to a discount of ten per centum on the amount of duty computed under such tariff, when such goods are conveyed without transshipment from a port of a country enjoying the benefits of the Britsh Preferential Tariff into a sea or river port of Canada.
Provided, however, that this discount shall not apply to duties on any of the following articles, viz., wines, malt liquors, spirits, spirituous liquors, liquid medicines and articles containing alcohol, sugar, tobacco, cigars and cigarettes.
Provided further that this discount shall not apply in the case in which the duty does not exceed fifteen per centum ad valorem, or, in the case of a specific duty or a specific and ad valorem duty combined in which the computed rate does not exceed fifteen per centum ad valorem, or to goods admitted into Canada which have the benefit of reductions provided for in the Canada-West Indies Trade Agreement, 1920.
2.	Resolved, that the Customs Tariff, 1907, be further amended by adding after section 8A the following as section 8B and 8C:-

8B. The Governor in Council may authorize any Minister of the Crown to enter into negotiations with any authorized representative of the government of the United States with a view to the making of a commercial agreement between the two countries on terms that may be deemed mutually beneficial. Any agreement so made Shall be subject to the approval of the parliament of Canada.
8C. If the President of the United States, under authority of the United States Tariff Act of 1922, determines to reduce by fifty per cent the duties imposed by such Act on the following articles, that is to say:
Cattle; wheat; wheat flour; oats, barley, potatoes, onions; turnips; hay; fish as enumerated in paragraphs 717, 718, 719 and 720 of the said Tariff Act of 1922, the Governor in Council may by order in council make such reductions of duties on similar articles imported into Canada from the United States as may be deemed reasonable by way of compensation for such reductions on Canadian products imported into the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I desire to change a word or two in paragraph 8C. It reads:
If the President of the United States, under authority of the United States Tariff Act of 1922, determine# to reduce by fifty per cent-
And so on. The American Tariff Act gives the President power to reduce by fifty per cent. It might be that he would make a reduction not of the full fifty per cent, and to meet that possibiliy I propose to leave out the words "by fifty per cent". The effect will be that if any reduction is made we shall be prepared to make corresponding reductions.

Before we come to the latter clause I wish to refer to a matter which relates to the first clause you read, Mr. Chairman. I submitted to the minister a situation which was brought to my attention by the Vancouver Board of Trade and asked him to give it his consideration. The point is that quantities of British goods are shipped via the Suez canal and transshipped at Hong Kong en route to the Pacific ports of Canada. The Canadian Pacific liners, for instance, and the Canadian Government Merchant Marine run their vessels from Vancouver and Victoria to Hong Kong. They rarely, except on special trips, run further, but they do proceed between these points regularly and they pick up merchandise which is brought by British vessels to Hong Kong. In that there is no violation of the spirit of this clause, but if the act is interpreted as at present I think the goods could not be shipped in that way and still obtain the benefit of the new provision. Will the minister say whether or not that point has been considered? [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Stevens) was kind enough to show me a communication he received on the subject, and later I received a similar communication. I have given the matter some consideration, but

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
the point raised is a debatable one and for the present I prefer to reserve a definite answer. If on further reflection it would seem desirable to interpret the clause in that way, I think the Governor in Council would have the power to do so. But we should like to give the matter further attention before making a definite reply.
Does my hon. friend not think that the Governor in Council has to be given the power to which he refers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the Governor in Council has the power now.
Under what resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not under any resolution here, but under the Tariff Act, which provides as follows:
The Governor in Council may by order in council extend the benefit of the British preferential tariff to any British country not named in paragraph (1) of section 3, and from and after the publication of such order in council in The Canada Gazette the British preferental tariff shall apply to goods the produce or manufacture of such British country, subject to the provisions of this act.
I think that is broad enough to give the government power; I am not sure we might not interpret it in that way without any further action. If it be a matter of debate I am persuaded the Governor in Council could so interpret the act at a later date. However, the point is new, and I would like to hear both sides of it before coming to a conclusion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question is on the first paragraph of the resolution, dealing with the British preferential tariff.

I appreciate any consideration the government may give to the matter, but I would point out that we are passing the resolution and I am apprehensive that we shall not have a later opportunity of discussing the point that I have raised. I am doubtful whether under the Customs Tariff Act that power is given to the Governor in Council. It gives the government power by order in council to apply similar provisions to other countries, but in this case we are dealing with the British colony port of Hong Kong, which is merely a transshipping point. I know this question is new; that is why I brought it to the minister's attention a few days ago. The minister says he is open to argument. Well, the point I wish to impress upon the committee is that such procedure as I have referred to would be no violation of the principle of this clause. The principle of the clause, as I understand it, is that British goods brought to Canadian ports shall have
the advantage of this reduction. But when it comes to our western ports the steamship lines do not travel the whole route without transshipment, and that is the point of the matter. If the minister would include the port of Hong Kong in the resolution-or perhaps it should be Singapore-it would cover the whole question and would give to the Pacific coast the advantage of this provision. If that is not done, I suppose two-thirds of the British goods coming to Canada via the Pacific will not come under this proviso. Let me emphasize the point by one further observation. Some of the old established British steamship lines-the Blue Funnel line, the Elder-Dempster line-run what they call the around-the-world route. Their ships start from Great Britain, call at Hong Kong and then go direct through the Panama canal or to the South American ports; but Canadian goods, British Columbia goods, are transshipped at Hong Kong. I think I have made it clear that no violation of the principle of this clause is involved and it seems to me that if a definite stipulation in this regard is not made, the government should take the power to do what the minister declares he will do if he is convinced of the merits of the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If we have not the power to deal with the matter, before the bill is finally through I will have it further investigated. I think we ought to have the power, and if it is not within our power now I will have an amendment considered at a later stage. Hong Kong is a British colony but it does not enjoy the British preference. If it were a preferential tariff colony, the case might be very simple. However, I do not wish to give judgment; the point is of sufficient importance to justify further consideration, and I would like to reserve decision on it. But if we have not power to deal with it by order in council I can give my hon. friend the assurance that power will be taken before this bill is finally through.

I rise to congratulate the government upon the adoption of this policy which has been very dear to my heart for a good many years. It is now nineteen years, I think, since I first introduced into this House a resolution embodying the principle of this part of our present tariff, and in 1907 I was able to move a resolution in amendment to the budget resolutions also embodying this policy. At that time, Mr. Chairman, it was accepted by the government as a principle, but the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, then Prime Minister, stated that it could not very
3456	COMMONS
Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
well be brought into force then because it would give a monopoly of transcontinental trade in British preferential goods to the one line of railway then constructed across this continent; but speaking upon this resolution and in moving an amendment thereto he said that it would be brought into force in December, 1911, when the National Transcontinental railway would be completed across this continent. Unfortunately, Mr. Chairman, in December, 1911, Sir Wilfrid Laurier had ceased to be Prime Minister, and so from that time until the present nothing has been done in the way of amending the British preferential tariff along this line. Last year I moved in this House a resolution embodying this policy, but advocating it be extended to the whole amount of the British preference. I regret that the present budget does not include my contention of last year in its entirety. I believe that the British preference in its entirety should be confined to goods brought into Canada through Canadian sea and river ports. But at last, Mr. Chairman, after long years, the principle has been adopted in the budget, and therefore it is that I feel personally pleased and very grateful to the government. I believe that even the ten per cent increase of British perference which will be allowed upon goods brought through Canadian sea and river ports will be of great benefit to the ports of the Maritime provinces. This is in line with the policy of building up Canadian trade which we have preached in this country since Confederation; it is in line with the policy of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier of building up our Canadian ports; and I only hope that in another year it will not be ten or twenty per cent, but that we shall finally adopt the policy of confining the British preference in its entirety to goods thus brought into Canada.

It seems to me that the policy of the government in this respect is rather unsound. I do not know why we should not have the advantage of the further reduction in the British preference on goods coming through American ports. I cannot sympathize, although I would like to with the remarks of the hon. member (Mr. Logan), who has just spoken. Of course, if he looks at the matter solely from the viewpoint of the inhabitants of some Nova Scotia ports, it is another matter, but looking at it from the viewpoint of the Canadian public I think the policy in this particular respect unsound, and I wonder how far it may result in the shipping of goods by the long haul instead of the short haul. The more direct route into the central part of Canada is, I think,

from Portland. I understand that there at least the traffic could be made tribute to what are now the Canadian National lines, whereas if the goods come through Halifax or St. John they will go over the Intercolonial railway by a very long route or over the Canadian Pacific from St. John to Montreal. I have not very much to say further, but I would like to express my dissent from the principle involved.
Mr. FORIvE: I would like at this particular point to express my appreciation of any preference that has been given to British imports. I think a great many of
4 p.m. our difficulties so far as marketing is concerned would be solved to a great extent had we a larger import trade from Great Britain. Great Britain is our principal market for all our surplus products, and if we could in some way purchase what we have to import from the British Isles we would have return cargoes and perhaps could do a more profitable trade.
In regard to the ten per cent increase in the British preference, while I appreciate the sentiments of the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) in respect to encouraging Canadian ports, it seems to me, looking at it from a western standpoint, that that ten per cent of British preference will be altogether blotted out by the increased transportation costs that will result from importing these goods through the Maritime ports and bringing them over the long haul westward. It is all very well this spirit of patriotism and encouraging our own ports, but when that is done at the expense of some other part of the country, it remains to be seen how much patriotism is in the matter after all. If we can find in the West that by the increased transportation cost over the long haul all the increase in the British preference is lost, then perhaps some excuse may be found for us if we are not very enthusiastic over the idea that is propounded in this scheme. It seems to me that if we are ever going to get anywhere both in taking our products to the market and in buying the stuff that we in this country want, the cheapest and the shortest haul will eventually be the one taken. I do not care for this trying to build things up artificially. It seems to me it will never get us anywhere. We must be prepared to do that which is best for all the people irrespective of what part of the country they happen to live in. In looking over the items I notice in the last clause dealing with cattle, wheat, wheat flour, oats, barley, potatoes, onions, turnips, hay and fish:
-as enumerated -in paragraphs 717, 718, 719 and 720 of the said Tariff Act of 1922, the Governor in Coun-

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
cil may by order in council make such reductions of duties on similar articles imported into Canada from the United States as may be deemed reasonable by way of compensation for such reductions on Canadian products imported into the United States.
I do not see any reason for that word "similar". I think the clause ought to read: make such reductions of duties on articles imported into Canada from the United States as may be deemed reasonable by way of compensation for such reductions on Canadian products imported into the United States.
Because in the articles here enumerated we have really no trade with the United States, and to insert the word "similar" takes away the meaning of the whole passage. I would move, Mr. Chairman, that the word "similar" be deleted from the resolution.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit us first to dispose of paragraph (1) dealing with the British preferential rate? That has not been disposed of by the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Just to show that this is not altogether a Maritime province question, I may say that one of the ideas in making the British preference applicable to Canadian ports was the hope that we might bring more ships to Canadian ports which would carry back across the water the products of Canada, and in that way divert to our Canadian ports some of the traffic that is now going to United States ports. Hon. members will surely understand that on the east the ports of Montreal and Quebec are nearer the West than the ports of Portland or New York, and on the west coast the port of Vancouver is nearer to the West. I submit it is more desirable that business should come into those ports than into the ports of Washington territory.
Why the necessity for putting in the paragraph? Why the necessity for making that regulation, if that is the proper route for them to take?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
With the hope that we will get vessels to carry away the products of our own country, and that we will get the long hauls for our own railways. My hon. friends must share in paying the losses we have been making upon our national railways, and if we can do anything to divert the long haul to our own railways, instead of shipping our wheat down to New York, if we can have more vessel space available at Canadian ports for that wheat, it seems to me that it will help not only the man on the prairies who is growing the wheat, but it will also help the eastern ports. It is not altogether a
Maritime question, it is a question affecting all Canada, in the hope that we may get greater revenues for our national railways.
Will wheat go to Montreal, if it is cheaper to go by some other port?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No; that is why we want to make it cheaper. We want more vessels in Montreal, and that will make it cheaper.

It seems to me the trade will go where it has been going most of the time. If you are going to increase the British preference 10 per cent, to bring goods from British ports, the chances are that increase on the cost will be paid by the people who buy the goods. I cannot see it any other way.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Excise
speechtext: Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: If they get it back in reduced freights from Canadian ports, they will be benefited.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Excise
speechtext: The distance is no greater between Montreal and the West than between Portland and the West. Then you have the lake route, or you can have an allrail route from Montreal, and St. John and Halifax all through the winter time.
Then why is it necessary to pass legislation to bring it about?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Excise
speechtext: To induce people to do it. The more ships you get in Canadian ports to carry back wheat to the Old Country, the more competition there is, and the lower the rate will be.

I am glad to see the British preference is reduced. It is to Britain that we shall have to look for many years to come for a market, particularly for our agricultural products, and while agricultural products are our chief exports from this country, the one thing to do, it seems to me, is to look for a return cargo, and the easier we make it, the surer we are of getting a return cargo. At the present time it is getting more unreasonable, as time goes on, to expect that our agricultural exports shall bear the cost of the trip both ways. With reference to the endeavour to compel British imports to come into Canadian ports, all I can tay is that the trade of this country, and the trade of all countries of the world, has to go in its natural channels, and no legislation can give any advantage to any Canadian port if it is cheaper to ship through other channels. I wish the government could have seen fit to increase the preference without any of these restrictions.

Of course I agree with the government in the policy of the British preference, because I think it is really an opportunity for the development of our Canadian ports. But the government saw fit to make exceptions in regard to certain articles which are not affected by the British preference. I observe in this resolution the discount shall not apply to duties on certain articles-wines, malt liquors, spirits and so on. But woollen articles are not included. I have in my hand a petition from some of my constituents concerning woollen goods, and of course they protest against the British preference on British woollen goods coming into Canada, and they state that this preference will be of no benefit to the woollen mills in Canada. They also say the commerce, especially of that section of my constituency in which they reside, will be very much affected by it. This petition expresses the opinion that the farmers in that part of my constituency, joining with the industries interested in the woollen mills, are in sympathy with that part of the petition which refers to Canadian woollen goods. I think this special industry in which the farmers are so interested should receive the special consideration of the government, and I cannot help lamenting that this preference is given to British goods.

The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) was not altogether correct in his remarks. He was quite right when he stated that he had been a constant and ardent advocate on the question of preference to our own ports, but he was quite wrong when he said nothing had been done towards crystallizing that principle in any way. For in the preferential agreement with the West Indies, in 1913 and again in 1920, there are sections covering this very question. Just confining my remarks for a moment to the question of the port, I want to ask my hon. friend the minister why it is right to extend the principle to 10 per cent-there is 10 per cent reduction in duty-while it is wrong to apply it in connection with the main British preference? It appears to me that the position as to each is exactly the same. The duties are the same, the articles are entirely the same. We have a further reduction made as a matter of principle. If that reduction has to be earned by going through Canadian ports, what is the minister's reason for withholding it from the larger question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not quite sure that I gather the hon. member's question. We are

making certain exceptions because the duties are low, is that the point?

No, the point
is this: In connection with the present 10 per cent reduction the government are congratulated by the hon. member for Cumberland upon having crystallized into action a principle, that principle being the carrying of Canadian commerce through Canadian channels. What I am trying to find out is this. Why is it that the principle applies only to this 10 per cent reduction and not to the general preference?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The idea is to bring a
gentle pressure to bear upon importers to ship by way of our own ports. We do not want to go so far as to say that they shall be penalized beyond the 10 per cent reduction for going to other ports. This is a gentle pressure to do the thing which we hope they will do anyway, but we do not want to be so drastic.
We are not getting the business. It is not coming.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This has not been tried yet.

I rather thought it had been tried, and if the minister consults the people who are engaged in the transportation business, he will find that they have done their best to get the trade. I was just wondering whether there was not another reason-that, in the opinion of my hon. friend, this provision would result in this 10 per cent not being taken advantage of. If my hon. friend wants to get the business, I cannot see why he starts with something that can be looked upon only as a pin-prick. Is not the real motive or is the real motive-I do not know which it is-that what is given with the one hand in this 10 per cent reduction is taken back with the other by this "Canadian port" provision?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is my hon. friend's unhappy way of putting the matter. I cannot put it more simply than I have. It is a gentle pressure to bring the goods through our own ports. We think this will come. If it does not come, experience will be the best teacher for us.
, I suppose we shall have to leave the matter in that way for the moment. The principle is wrong-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What principle is wrong?

The principle
of the "Canadian port" is wrong when applied

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
in connection with the lower duty which might bring results. It is right when we have it dealt with in connection with this 10 per cent reduction. The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans) pointed out something which I thought would have weighed a good deal with my hon. friend. I confess that the hon. member for Saskatoon, after having made the argument, did not apply it. He pointed out that at present agriculture is carrying the cost both ways on the ocean trip, because we do not have proper return cargoes. I thought he would have been greatly interested, therefore, in seeing that there were return cargoes to our Canadian ports where we could have proper methods of control in connection with grain movements. That, however, may be something which the minister will consider further in making up his mind whether it is possible to make this something real or not.
What does my hon. friend think as regards the position of the woollen mills? In the first instance, I would ask him whether he found any decrease in the cost of woollen articles during the past year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think there was any decrease. Of course, I would not like to 'answer that definitely. The question of the cost did not quite enter into our minds in this matter. If my hon. friend means: Are the woollen mills satisfied with this?-frankly, no, they are not.
I do not mean that. I asked my hon. friend if there had been any difference, since his last budget was brought down, in the cost of woollens to the consumer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would not like to
answer that. I am not aware that there has been.
My hon. friend is very wise in not answering-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps so.

-because the
figures of the Labour bureau, if I read them aright-and I am willing to accept at once any correction that comes from my hon. friend or his expert, if I read them wrongly- show that there has been an actual increase in the cost of woollen goods to the Canadian consumer.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Has there not been an increase in the cost of the raw material-wool?
My hon. friend answers one question by asking another.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He is Irish.

I am dealing simply with one thing at a time. There has been an increase in cost, notwithstanding the fact that my hon. friend reduced the duty on woollens last year and increased the preference. Does my hon. friend know-and again I am going to accept his figures-if it is a fact in connection with woollens, having regard to the textiles turned out, that the yardage has decreased and importations have increased by about 52 per cent, I think the figures are?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There has been an increase; I have not the figures at hand. If the cost of woollens has increased in the meantime, might that not be a reason why an effort should be made to reduce the cost by reducing the duty?
The unfortunate thing is that the cost went up with the reduction in the duty.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Then we will increase the duty in order to reduce the cost.
I hear an echo from my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: That is the logic of the matter.

We might as well deal with things as they turn out. It might be that the taxes on Canadian business, the added burden of production in this country, are the real reasons why we have so much more importation coupled with a higher price. Will my hon. friend dispute this figure that there has been an increase of over 52 per cent in the importations of woollen textiles.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There has been some increase. I do not quite see the bearing of this on my hon. friend's question as regards reducing the rates of duty.
Does my hon. friend desire to increase that importation at the present time by lowering the duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would like to increase the importation and to increase the manufacture at the same time, in order that all business might be promoted and encouraged.
Does my hon. friend know how that can be done?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a matter of opinion.

Does my hon. friend know that the textile mills in Canada- and we heard from one of them in Quebec to-day-are working on an average only 30 per cent of their time, so that the net result

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
is that Canadian workmen are working 30 per cent of their time, importations are increased accordingly 52 per cent, and the public are paying a higher price? Does my hon. friend want to aggravate that situation?
Would the hon. member increase the duty and have another mill started?

That question, of course, I do not think my hon. friend is very serious about. It is a splendid thing to have a real sense of Scotch humour, but at present I do not know that my hon. friend is doing much more than making a joke. New mills?-of course not; unless something occurs in this country to improve conditions, we shall not need any mills at all. What is the use of talking about putting up new mills when our own mills are not operating more than 30 per cent of their time?
That is just what I was wondering.
What is the price of knitted woollens since my hon. friend's last budget? Did they go up or down?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will let my hon. friend answer if that affords him satisfaction.

No. I look
upon this as a serious question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Certainly.

I would have
thought my hon. friend had studied Canadian conditions with a view of seeing what ought to be done in connection with his fiscal changes. I would have thought he would know conditions; I think he does know, and I again ask him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I assure my hon. friend that we have considered all conditions. I never knew a time when an interest touched by the tariff did not become alarmed. Honestly and sincerely, I have no doubt, the woollen mills to-day are disturbed. I hope and believe that with the improved condition of business which is near at hand, their fears will prove to be mistaken. There is no industry which you touch in the tariff which does not represent to you that it is placed in peril. I quite respect the views of these manufacturers. I have been through a similar experience in days gone by. But I am glad to know that in most cases their anticipations of disaster proved unfounded. I hope it will be so in this case.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister has been through a similar experience, he says. He did in the previous case what he will do here if he is in power; when in power before he put the woollen duties down to 23 or 23i per cent. Everything that was predicted at that time happened ; everything that was foretold from the opposition benches took place. He destroyed about half the woollen industry of the country, while he did not help the woollen consumer at all. With what result? He came back to parliament a few years afterwards and admitted that he had gone too low and that instead of helping the country he had hurt it. He therefore asked parliament at that time to restore the woollen duties back to 30 per cent, which rate just kept the woollen industries in existence. They have struggled along, but they have not done more than that. There are a great many of them; there is not just one large concern, but a goodly number have been kept in existence under the duty which the hon. gentleman decided to restore after an experience which alone could teach him. I suspect that he is travelling around the circle again at the expense of the people of the country; he will again learn by experience, but the people will suffer. He will realize his mistake after perhaps two or three years, and at a very great cost not only to the Canadian woollen producers, but to the Canadian consumer as well. What happens is this: The outside goods come in and displace the Canadian product; those goods are able to do this through the lower tariff. And this having happened, the Canadian manufacturers are forced to limit their hours of work, while their overhead goes up and their unit costs of production increase; and with each such increase the outsider gets the benefit because he is competing against a crippled industry. That is what the minister himself discovered twenty years ago. Why should he have to be taught it all over again? The reason is just in order that he may do his share of the log-rolling to get his budget through the House.
I hope the minister will be benefited by the advice he is getting.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: He will benefit by "experience."

It seems that this tale of the woollen manufacturers is a pitiful one indeed. I would tell my good friend, the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) that one of the tragedies of Mark Twain's life was that people would not take him seriously. Now, I want the hon. gentleman to take me seriously; I am not joking. One of the troubles in

Ways and Means-Customs Tarifi
connection with this industry is the inability of the people to purchase. There has never been any over-production; so far as I can see, the difficulty has always been in underconsumption. If the people could buy these goods there would be a market for all the woollen goods produced in Canada as well as for woollen imports. I wonder if my hon. friend knows how many people in this cold climate are obliged to go without proper underclothing in winter because of high prices?
I do not think that increasing the tariff will help that condition of affairs in any way.

I really thought that my hon. friend was joking when he referred to a new mill at the present time. I want to pay this tribute to him, however, that although he jokes he always does so delightfully. He must be joking, too, when he talks about the present situation. Does he think that he improves the purchasing power of the poor people by making woollen goods dearer, as we had them last year, with the Canadian mills not operating? There is no good purpose to be served by talking generalities; the simple fact is that the rates went up materially. I will ask the minister whether that was not true in connection with woollen knitted goods? My information is that it is absolutely correct; I am informed that the prices went up. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A great many articles went up in price, but I do not see what that has to do with the question of the duties that are to be levied.
I am trying to get at the facts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member knows what the facts are; there is no need for him to ask me.
Is this correct or not,-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You say it is correct, and I have not disputed it.
Is this correct-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Probably not.
-that the importation of knitted goods increased in bulk over one hundred per cent-I think it was 104 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It may be so; I have not the figures before me. But of what consequence is it?
Can the ex-Minister of Finance tell us why these mills are shut down?

It is generally
known that the woollen industry, things being as they are in this country, is worked from the top down rather than from the bottom up, as it should be. The woollen industry has to go to Bradford for its tops, there being no place in Canada where our own raw materials could be put into proper shape for our manufacturers.

I thought that was the
cheapest place of all.

Well, let us see what happens at Bradford. As I recollect, before the war Bradford converted woollen tops at an average of a penny half-penny; I am not sure of the figure, but I think it was around that sum; and the price of the tops was something around sixpence. Now, there is a combination in Bradford between the man who knits the tops and the man in the other branch of the business; and when Canadians have to pay an advance in the price of tops from 200 to 300 per cent, it is not difficult to see where the trouble lies. With wages in Canada much higher than they were in England, it is not hard, either, to realize the difficulties that our manufacturers have had to face. We have a mill started now; I do not know whether it has actually started, but at all events there is1 a mill being built at Trenton to-day. If that mill is allowed to get going and is properly operated, if it is not put out of business by sales taxes and cheque taxes, by this thing and the other thing, we ought to be able to get cheap tops in



Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
Canada on the one hand, and a decent price for Canadian woollens, on the other. There is no secret to-day as to why the Canadian woollen industry requires protection; the reason that these concerns are going out of business is simply that the protection has been cut down. They are working thirty per cent of their time, while they have to face an increase of one hundred per cent in imports' in knitted goods. If the minister is satisfied with such a state of affairs, I do not know that the committee can do anything by detaining him very much longer. He does not seem to be concerned about these tremendous increases in our imports; he does not seem to be moved by any consideration such as, for example, the fact that these businesses are running thirty per cent of time. And as a corollary, it is obvious that it does not in the least affect him that an industrial exodus from this country is now going on,- we need not wonder why.

I am assured that the difference will not bring to us any decrease in the price of material. But there is another matter of interest in this: If we close down our woollen mills we are certainly putting our wool at a disadvantage because we are permitting the importation of material manufactured from the wool of southern countries, and it is a well-known fact that this wool will produce a finer fabric than the wool of northern countries. This is a matter of great importance to our agriculturists.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend has given us some interesting theories of political economy. It is quite fairly established by the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) that if you reduce duties you are increasing prices; that is his argument. We reduced the duties on certain goods in the budget a year ago. and the prices of such goods have increased; that is cause and effect, he says. That is a new doctrine altogether, and I give my hon. friend the benefit of it. Let us not misunderstand him. We reduce the duties and thereupon the prices increase; therefore you should not reduce the duties. I remember some years ago in a debate of that kind when a distinguished statesman was advancing the argument that by increasing duties they had reduced prices, a small boy interrupted "If you had only doubled the duties we would have got the goods for nothing." That is the logical result of my hon. friend's argument. My hon. friend distinctly declares that by reducing duties I am increasing prices. I am sure for the sake of his 
reputation my hon. friend does not wish to be taken seriously.
He is joking.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am suddenly discovering that these tariff changes are of vast concern and importance. I understood from the speeches in this House and elsewhere not long ago that the changes made were insignificant. Hon. gentlemen opposite could hardly find words sufficiently small to indicate the insig-ficance of the duties; but now we are discovering that these insignificant, trifling duties are destroying the industries of the country. So I am getting some new theories of political economy. I let my hon. friend, the ex-Minister of Finance, have his own statistics, I do not question them. He is advancing the view that large importations of woollen goods are injurious to the country. We have admitted for last year an importation of wearing apparel and knitted goods amounting to $472,-000-a large sum. I can imagine my hon. friend picturing to the woollen people of the country the awful evil that came to them by the importation of that one year. But if he will turn back to the year 1921, when the country had the good fortune of having the guidance of my hon. friend as Minister of Finance he will find the importation not $472,000 but $890,000. Now then, what happened? If the woollen industry of the country is bad under this importation of $470,000, what must it have been in 1921 under an importation nearly double?

I wonder if my hon. friend is dealing with the latest figures?
I said I was prepared for correction, I invited it. I want to try and get at the truth in connection with these matters. We too often have general statements made and not enough facts behind them. I stated what I had been told and I asked my hon. friend for the information.

Mr. Chairman, may I submit to the hon. member for West York and others also the danger of being led into a fallacy when comparing the prices of woollens now with the prices at some time in the past when the general price level may have shifted in the meantime?

Quite right.

Does not that refer to the Dominion Textiles?

I was disappointed that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) did not in his budget propose a larger increase in the British preference, particularly on cotton goods. I think if there is one thing the people of this country are entitled to it is cheaper cotton goods, because very often they cannot afford to buy woollen goods, but as things stand we are making it exceedingly difficult for them to get even cotton clothing. This article says, in regard to Penman's and Textile:
Montreal.-Here are two stocks that have shown rather startling increases in their market values during the past year. Penman's which sold at 99 in 1922, is now at 159 and recently touched the highest point in its history.
That does not sound pessimistic.
The stock is paying 8 per cent this year, including a bonus of 2 per cent paid in February and taking this as the dividend return the yield to the investor at 159 is about 6.30 per cent, not a very high yield for a common stock. Dominion Textile during 1922 sold as low as 133. To-day's market prices are about 68 and allowing for the "three to one split" early in the year-
I hope hon. gentlemen will take note of that.
-this is the equivalent of 215 for the old stock. Dominion Textile's dividend rate is 12 per cent for the old stock, $4 a share on the new and the yield is 5.90 per cent, which is very low.
It is obvious, therefore, that the investor who buys either Dominion Textile or Penman's is looking for something beyond the present income return. There is justification for believing that these additional attractions are in the offing for both securities.
Penman's may follow the example of Dominion Textile and divide its stock into 'smaller units. There are disadvantages in having a stock selling at too high a price.
I suppose one of the disadvantages, Mr. Chairman, is this: That it makes it a little bit harder, or it takes a little more nerve, to go to the Finance Minister and ask for further protection for that particular industry.
Penman's at 157 has a somewhat restricted market that would be broadened if, for instance, a new company were formed that gave each shareholder two or three shares of stock perhaps of no par value for each $100 share he now holds. The number of shares available for trading would be increased and an increase in the dividend might be more likely. Now this scheme of dividing up Penman's stock has not been decided upon; but it i3 just what was done in the case of Dominion Textile and it is what many investors are looking for and it is because so many investors look for something of this kind that the stock has advanced to its present point.
It seems to me that it is time we got some worth while reduction of the tariff on some particular lines, and these are two of the lines on which a reduction is due to the people of Canada.

Remember, Mr. Chairman, that this is stock which has recently been split up to the extent of three shares for one.

Since 1920 earnings have not been so great, but increased in 1922 over the previous year.
Apparently the little reduction that the Finance Minister made last year did have the effect of increasing the earning power of this woollen industry.
The working capital position is excellent and the company has liquid investments greater than the amount of its bonds outstanding.
Dominion Textile has almost as excellent a record earning during the past five years a total of 116 per cent, out of which dividends, totalling only 45 per cent, were paid. This meant that 71 per cent went back into the business. There has been a steady sure growth to Textile's earnings.
When two stocks are selling at the highest levels in their history and have discounted, marketwise, the possible developments, is that the time for the investor to purchase thftn? A lot depends upon the general business and investment outlook. Be it said though that both Penman's and Dominion Textile are common stocks that offer a wealth of real assets that have demonstrated an ability to earn a substantial margin above dividends paid. They are both capably managed, the president of each company being the same able executive, Sir Charles Gordon. They are operating in a field that has not been overdone and that is practically controlled by Canadian mills with little competition from foreign firms, to some extent due tq the tariff.

What has that got to do with it?

A great deal. I will tell my hon. friend in a moment what it has to do with it. The Dominion Cotton Mills at that time was not in a good condition, and it was only by excellent and careful management that the Dominion Textile Company is in the position it is in to-day-no other reason at all.

I would remind my hon. friend that the Financial Post suggests that part of this prosperity may be due to the tariff. I think possibly it is only fair to Senator McSweeney in view of what the hon. member says, that I read his statement.
I think that would hardly be fair. The hon. member has dealt with that.

If the business people of Canada, those engaged in the various manufacturing industries, found they could not survive without a reduction of the British preference, and the mills had to close up as a consequence, would the hon. member approve of that? In other words, would he prefer to have the tariff reduced and the mills closed?
I submit to this House, and to the hon. member who has asked the question, that I do not think it is a fair question at all.
Why?

Because I do not think any man should admit that the cotton industry or the woollen industry could not survive with a 10 per cent tariff. Let me ask my hon. friend this question: If 75 per cent of the people engaged in the agricultural industry, or of the people engaged in the industry of growing wheat, were to come to this House and say "We cannot produce wheat at a profit at the present prices which we receive for our wheat and at the present prices which we must pay for everything we buy which goes into that wheat," would my hon. friend opposite be willing to reduce the tariff to secure a lower cost of living? Apply that principle to the woollen and cotton industry. Would the hon. member agree that those who are engaged in growing wheat should have cheaper cottons and cheaper woollens, so that the prices they are getting for their wheat would allow them to purchase these things? I think that is a fairer question than the one the hon. member propounded to me.

My hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote) is very much mistaken in his first observation that increasing the British preference would give us cheaper cotton goods. I did not wish to speak on cotton goods, but I would like to make an observation on that item. During last year the importation of knitted cotton goods from the

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
United Kingdom was very small. We imported only 20,319 pairs of cotton socks and stockings from the United Kingdom, but we imported 544,538 pairs of cotton socks and stockings from the United States; so that the British preference plays very little part in the matter of importation of cotton hosiery.

If the present tariff charge against hosiery from Great Britain were cut in two would we bring any more hose from Great Britain, or would the Canadian manufacturer simply meet the price and go on manufacturing?

I am speaking of the importation of cotton hosiery. It would not make any difference in the cost of cotton hosiery if the British preference were increased, because the cotton hosiery does not come from Great Britain, but from the United States. But I rose to point out that in the knitting mill business in the province of Ontario there are employed a very fine class of Canadian citizens, under conditions quite different from the conditions prevailing in the Old Land. The mills in the province of Ontario are conducted under regulations which are advantageous to Canadian workmen and conditions that do not apply in the Old Land, and the Canadian manufacturers of knitted goods in the small towns of Ontario and in my own constituency are paying fifty per cent more wages than the current rate of wages in Scotland and England. We are working under a minimum wage law; we are working under the Workmen's Compensation Act and the Factory Inspection Act, all of which we are strongly in favour of, in order that the work men and working women may be placed under the best working conditions. There are hon. members in this House who came from Great Britain, and who came to this country to find better conditions, and we have them here. The only protection, or the only consideration, that the knitting mills of the province are asking is a tariff which will offset the additional labour costs they are bearing in Ontario. Beyond that they ask for nothing. I will point out to my hon. friends that $100 worth of merchandise represents about $40 worth of labour, or $20 need of protection. That is the actual protection that is needed for labour. Then again there is the duty on machinery and the sales tax on wool which is being removed by the Finance Minister's budget. The knitting mills in Ontario require just that much protection for that purpose, and if hon. members are fair with regard to tariff matters, and with regard to British preference, they must take into consideration this one vital point-do you
want your Ontario workmen, or your workman for that matter from any other part of the Dominion, to maintain the conditions under which he is working or do you want him to meet the competitive wages of Great Britain?

If the
Ontario workmen are enjoying better conditions in their work than the British workmen, would they not to that extent be more efficient?

I can answer the question this way, that the efficiency of the workmen in a hosiery mill is not so much a factor as my hon. friend might suggest. It is a business, largely of automatic machinery; the machinery mostly all is imported. The worker's efficiency is regulated entirely by the machinery, and the conditions are identical in Scotland and in Canada, because our knitting mills have installed during the past few years the very best type of Scottish and English equipment. The machinery is exactly the same and the speed of operators, I am told by those who have studied the question, varies but little between the British and Canadian mills. The knitted goods men in this country point out that under last year's tariff there was a large increase in the importation of knitted goods from the Old Land, but I do not think they objected seriously to that. But this year they point out that the importation of hosiery from Great Britain will not arrive in this country at any lower price than last year under the tariff existing last year. One hundred dollars' value in hosiery last year paid $25 duty and $4.69 sales tax, or a total value of $129.69. Under the new tariff it pays for $100 value, $22.50 duty and $7.35 sales tax, a total value of $129.85, or 16 cents additional on $100 value. The domestic manufacturer under the old tariff would receive $100 plus the sales tax $2.25, making a total cost of $102.25 to the retailer. Under this new tariff his value was $100, but he must take credit for the saving of 3| per cent on his wool value of $50, making a saving of $1.88. Then he adds a sales tax of 6 per cent, which is $5.89. His total cost is $104.01, or an increase in cost of $1.76. In other words we are not delivering the British article at as low a price as we did last year. In fact, the price is 16 cents more and we are taking out of the Canadian knit goods manufacturer $1.76 or If per cent. Hon. gentlemen might think that was a very small thing, but on behalf of the small hosiery mills, I should like to say that 10 cents a dozen p urs is considered a good profit for the mill. Ten cents a dozen pairs will give a mill a reason-
