ably large earning. When there is no actual saving to the public by the new tariff condition, there is a good deal to be said in favour of these mills when a load of $1.76 per one hundred dollars is put upon them because in the total aggregate that load amounts practically to the earnings of their mills.
My hon. friend made some statements about earnings of cotton or textile mills. I am not inclined to doubt his statements but on behalf of the smaller industries in Ontario which are vital to the life of many of the small towns, industries which are financed without any watered stock, with the invested capital of men who have made all their own money and who have made it in the industries, I submit to my hon. friends this one consideration, that in applying a reduction of 50 per cent in the British preference, they would succeed in closing or making it impossible to work many of the finest and most hopeful small industries in Ontario, and that they would not give them the protection to which they are entitled owing to the different wages paid and the different standards of living asked for by provincial regulations. This is a point that my hon. friends must consider in dealing with these tariff matters and it is the only viewpoint I take with regard to the question. We talk a good deal about our living conditions in Canada and we hope to attract workmen and other men besides, by these better conditions which we offer them. That is correct. But if on the one hand we press for a certain condition and a certain rate of wages, and on the other we lower the rate of duty so that the payment of that rate of wages will not be permitted, we are leaving our workmen and our manufacturers between the upper and the nether millstones, so that they cannot survive.

If I might use the words of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) my hon. friend, if I understood him correctly, made the bald statement that wages were 50 per cent higher in our Canadian mills than they were in Great Britain. Would he give this committee some statistics to show that that is the case?

I am sorry I cannot give the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) the exact figures; but I can assure him that I will secure them for him and that the statement is quite correct that in the knitting industry in Ontario wages are 50 per cent higher than in the knitting industry in Scotland and England. I think the piece work wage for men in Scotland is about $11 [Mr. Malcolm.!
or $12 a week and the day wage is slightly less. I would rather not quote, because I am speaking from memory and I am not quite sure as to the figures. I shall however be glad to procure the figures for my hon. friend this afternoon. I have the figures in my office.
Would my hon. friend be good enough to give the committee also some idea of the difference in the cost of living in England and Canada?
I have no doubt the cost of living has a direct bearing on the cost of labour. That does not enter into this argument at all.

I rise in the first instance to congratulate the hon. member for North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm). He has given us a first rate exposition of what, ought to be the underlying principles of the budget. He has shown us that the protective feature ought to be and must be considered, that is of course if we are going to continue to function. He has shown us that he has no use whatever for that old bugaboo of a "tariff for revenue" which really never buga-booed at all. He has shown us that we ought to have consideration on the one hand of the cost to the consumer and on the other to the returns to the workmen. He has gone further; he has shown us very clearly what the effect of a muddled view of these things is. He has shown us for example that on the one hand there is less protection to the Canadian workmen, and on the other hand there is greater cost to the Canadian consumer. I was going to say-and I would not have said it nearly as well-something along the'same lines in answer to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) when he said, "This is a new doctrine and a new theory-advance tariffs and you get lower rates; cut them and you have higher rates." The whole thing runs together; there is only one issue here- the fiscal policy as a whole. At one time, for example, practically all tin plate utilized in the United States-my hon. friend knows this just as well if not better than I do-was imported, all the costs of transportation paid, all the costs of handling at the ports paid, and then a far higher rate was paid than you can buy tin-plate for to-day in the States. It is also true that by a high tariff costs were temporarily increased largely; but it is also true that it was not so very many years before those people were exporting that tin-plate, and that high tariff has very greatly reduced the cost in that country. It is also, of course, true that if

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
you have enough people who are engaged in active competition one with another, you are getting your prices pretty well regulated in your local market. It is also true that those prices can be proper prices only if you have something like a proper volume of business. If you have not a proper volume of business and are working only 30 per cent of your time, your overhead must go up, just as happened last year with that reduction in the duty. It is also true that the English sellers, selling as they do in this market, take precious good care that the Canadian consumer does not get all the benefit of the Canadian preference, but the benefit of the preference goes to the man who is in the position to collect it, as he is just as soon as local production is down to such a point that local costs have to go up. There is no mystery about the thing. The Minister of Finance is extremely agile in taking one or two disconnected instances and having a "hurrah" on them; he is a perfect adept at that. He is an absolute wizard at the art of misrepresenting an argument; he is a wonderful politician. But just see how the hon. member for North Bruce answers him. Why, he says, under this budget-and he gives the exact figures-while you are reducing protection and, therefore, taking away the work from your own people, you are adding to the cost. It is all very well to have a trifling reduction, and I still say that the reductions in the mass were trifling. But if there is anything in this idea about cutting and slashing tariffs, the object should be to reduce prices. A little niggling reduction here and another one there is not going to do very much except to disturb Canadian industrial conditions; it is not going to reflect itself to any extent in reduced prices to the Canadian consumer. At any rate, that is what we have found. When my hon. friend comes down here and makes a tariff reduction on the one hand and then plusses it with a sales tax much greater on the other hand, what else is to be expected? Everyone knows that every word said by the hon. member (Mr. Malcolm) is absolutely correct; the figures are there and they cannot be disputed. An hon. gentleman opposite shakes his head. If he can discover how a reduction in the cost of living is brought about by a per cent or 3 per cent, or if you like, a 4 per cent reduction of duty on the one hand, and a sales tax of 6 per cent on the other hand, I cannot see it. The minister is an adept at putting the other fellow in the wrong.

speechtext: When he is wrong.
He does it beautifully, and the other fellow need not be wrong at all. Now, I am going to go back to what I said before.

speechtext: "Far away from harm."

Well, I think
that if we did go there we should get more facts than we have got this afternoon. I will take the figures dealing exactly with the matters 1 submitted to my hon. friend. These figures are prepared from the records of the monthly reports of the trade of Canada for ten months ending January 23, 1923, and a proportional allowance is made to give the figures up to the end of March, the comparison being as at the end of March 1922 and 1923. The next matter I took up was hosiery and socks. For the year ending March, 1922, there were 257,089 dozen pairs imported into Canada; for the year ending March, 1923, there were 610,372 dozen pairs imported, or an approximate increase, not of 104 per cent, as I thought, but 138 per cent. These are the figures I have, and as I have said, the source from which they come is to be found in the monthly reports of the trade of Canada. I believe they are absolutely correct, and the very shutting down of the mills would show that they are.

The hon. member (Sir Henry Drayton) has made many criticisms regarding the closing down of mills and the suspension of operations, and the bearing of these conditions on the prices of woollen goods throughout Canada. I believe that neither the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) nor the woollen industry is to blame for this serious state of affairs. The fact is that within the past few months the great woollen industries of New England have invaded Canada and have purchased every pound of wool that has been available. They bought not only what was in storage throughout the country but what was on the backs of the sheep, for which they contracted. No doubt the mills have had to suspend operations, and we can easily explain the situation by taking as an analogy the wheat industry, for instance. When wheat is high, flour and other wheat products must necessarily be high at the same time. And the same thing holds true in regard to rubber. If a great rubber enterprise is strong enough to go abroad and contract for raw rubber at very low prices, the rubber industry generally must be affected. But not all the rubber concerns can do this' and our woollen mills in Canada could not have anticipated such enterprise on the part of industries that had been closed down in the United States for years; they could not have anticipated that these industries would be in a position to come into Canada and forestall them. So that I do not see that anyone can blame the Minister of Finance. My hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) has repeatedly asked the minister the question: "Are you not aware that the prices of woollen goods are increasing? Do you not know that several of the mills have, had to close down?" Well, had these mills been able to secure their raw material and circumvent the action of the New England industries, conditions would no doubt have been different to-day. That is the situation as I see it, and I believe I have stated it correctly.

I wish to protest against this change in the British preference; I believe that the continual reduction of the preference from year to year will have but one effect, and that will be disaster. What we are faced with now is a competition between the standards of living of the British workmen and of the Canadian factory hand. The Canadian manufacturer, under the conditions forced upon him by these reductions, is bound to reduce costs. Coming from a constituency in which there are about four factories making woollen and knitted goods, I am naturally more or less interested in this question. I re-
ceived a letter from one of them this morning stating that there had been a great increase in the importation of knitted and woollen goods from Great Britain since the change in the duty last year, and also pointing out that at the present time all the woollen mills in this country are experiencing the keenest competition they have ever known. As soon as the manufacturer is faced with the necessity of reducing costs, he has, among other things, to reduce wages. If his factory is working only part-time, perhaps four or five days a week, the pay envelope of the worker is very much reduced, and he in turn is forced to decide between remaining where he is or going where he can get a better living. And it does not take long for the Canadian worker to decide when to move over to the United States, particularly under present conditions. Very many members of the House deplore the fact that a number of Canadian workers have gone to the United States in the last six months, and it seems to me that a change in the tariff such as is now proposed accelerates rather than retards this exodus. After we have accomplished that we spend large sums of money inducing immigrants to come to this country and then move through the same circle all over again.

I have a good deal of sympathy with hon. members who have spoken along this line. I should like, however, to ask them: Have they ever taken into consideration the standard of living of the people who are engaged in an industry that has to compete against all the world, that has no protection whatever? The most poorly paid labour in the world can compete with our agriculturists in the production of the staple article which they have to sell in the world's market. That is one primary fact that we must get into our minds to start with. I listened with a good deal of interest to the hon. member for North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm). He always speaks sanely and moderately, and I have no doubt he is quite sincere in his statements regarding our small woollen manufacturers. I saw an article in the Montreal Gazette the other day which no doubt contains a certain amount of truth, although I cannot vouch for it. It mentions that a box of apples packed by a Perth farmer brought him 40 cents. He placed a ticket in the box asking the purchaser to advise him what price he paid for the contents, and in due time he received a letter from a farmer in Saskatchewan stating that the apples had cost him $2.60. There you have the great spread between 40 cents and $2.60. When the hon. member for North Bruce stated that 10 cents

Ways and Means-Customs Tarif!
was a fair profit for the manufacturer on a dozen pair of stockings I should like him to have told us the retail price of a pair of such stockings. No doubt the information would be very interesting. I think a great many of our difficulties are due to this unreasonable spread between the price received by the producer and that paid by the consumer.
I should like to see our manufacturers and our farmers get a little closer together in order that they may the better understand each other's problems. I have no ill feeling towards the manufacturers.' It seems to be a generally accepted idea that we are fighting the manufacturers. This is not the case. We are fighting a system that we do not think is working out to the best interests of the people. I stated quite recently that the cost of living here is as high as it is in any other part of the world, whereas this ought to be one of the cheapest countries to live in. This is one reason why we cannot compete successfully in manufacturing. A good deal has been said this afternoon about the standard of living in the Old Land. It is forty years since I left Scotland. I knew a great deal about the woollen mills of Galashiels and other centres, having come from the border counties, and I can tell you, Mr. Chairman, that at that time the condition of the workers in those mills was just as good as the condition of the farmers on the plains of Manitoba to-day. So when the cost of living is blamed on the farmers I resent it. I question if there is very much difference between the conditions in that woollen district and in our maunfacturing districts to-day except in the cost of living. If a worker in the mills here or a mechanic wants to buy a cottage it costs him a large amount of money, and the cost of his food and clothing is also very high. Consequently, his living expenses being very high, the employer must pay him correspondingly high wages, and therefore is unable to compete successfully with the manufacturers in other parts of the world. We have a vicious system working in a vicious circle, and it seems to me that we are never going to get out of it, for apparently my hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton), like Ephraim, is "wedded to his idols."
I want to remove the idea that we are hostile to the manufacturing interests merely for the sake of hostility. I am always glad to see our manufacturers prospering. I should like to see all our manufacturing industries prosper, but if this is to be at the expense of the other sections of the community which, I claim, are engaged in the basic industries of our country, then I demur. I had a gentleman this day seriously proposing to me a minimum price for wheat. He was of opinion that if the farmers of this country could be assured of a price to cover the cost of production Canada would become enormously prosperous in the very near future because such a great impulse would be given to production. This proposal is not so absurd as it may appear at first sight once you look into it. When we remember how often we are told that it is absolutely necessary for our manufacturing industries to be helped along, why should the farmers on the prairie provinces continue to produce wheat at a loss to feed the poor people on the continent of Europe?
Does the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) consider he would have done just as well had he remained working in the woollen mills of Scotland instead of coming to Canada?

I never worked in the woollen mills of Scotland. I can tell my hon. friend the advice I got before I left the Old Land to come to Canada, and that was: Go where there is money. And being of the type that I am it is most likely that I would get it.
And you got itT
I am glad to say, Mr. Chairman, that knowing the Old Flag waved over Canada, I decided to become a Canadian. I am here, and I want everyone to understand that I am a Canadian through and through.

I have been very much interested in the figures quoted by those who have preceded me. The ex-Minister of Finance, (Sir Henry Drayton), pointed out that for the year ending March 1922, we imported 12,208,523 yards of woollen goods, worth $472,
000.	This amounts to only 6 cents per capita of our population. For the following year ending March 1923, the importation amounted to 18,793,613 yards worth $962,000, or under 10 cents per capita. It looks to me as if the two old parties are vieing with each other and spending much time trying to assure the manufacturers that their interests will be well looked after. Relatively speaking, these importations are trifling. When the manufacturers ask for protection they do not produce their books, they do not get down to business and prove that they really need protection. We are held up as a party that believes in ruining the manufacturing industries. That is altogether wrong. We want to see industries of all kinds prospering in this country, for we realize that it is to the national benefit that industries native to the country

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
should be prosperous. But we want to have a little share in the prosperity. I know there are Canadian industries making big dividends to-day. The secretary-treasurer of one particular industry told me that for twenty-five years they have never earned less than 20 per cent, and in some years even 50 per cent, and the stockholders have never got less than 10 per cent cash dividend; yet that industry is highly protected.
What is the name?

I am not going to enter into personalities. Other speakers have not given facts about their business, and I am not going to divulge personal confidences. But this discussion has been carried on this afternoon over relatively small matters, and as far as the tariff is concerned they look to me to be of no importance. The hon. member for North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm) said that 72,000 dozen pairs of cotton stockings had been imported from Great Britain in 1922 and 962,000 dozen from the United States. Well, what does that amount to when you come to consider the population? It is one dozen pairs for every seven or eight people in the country. I think we are spending a, good deal of time over the woollen and cotton manufacturers that is not getting us anywhere.

I do not want to throw discredit upon statistics, especially those of the Customs department. But here is a very interesting point that is worth mentioning while we are on the subject, especially having regard to the warning of the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) that we must deal with quantities, not values. Mr. Chairman, I wish to
make some observations on a few of the remarks that have been made during the last hour and a half. It is quite true that the problems we have been discussing are complicated. One of the causes of difficulty is the problem of distribution; the tariff is another item. I think it is just as well to remember that there may be a number of causes which give rise to a particular situation. Attention has been drawn this afternoon to the present industrial conditions in the United States, and I want to suggest that it is a pertinent question for us to ask ourselves why there has been an improvement in industrial conditions in that country, while there has not been such an improvement here. I am not going to answer that question, but it is a very pertinent one. We may interpret the facts quite differently. We may say it is due to tariff conditions when it may be due to entirely different conditions.
With regard to the standards of living, the hon. member for London (Mr. White) has

Ways and Means-Customs TarvJ
made the statement that the protective tariff is necessary for us to preserve a certain standard of living in this country. Now so far as the farmers are concerned, the Canadian farmer competes freely in the open market with the producers of India, who live on an entirely different standard, and I submit to the hon. member that we have to take into consideration the efficiency of the people who work and live under different conditions. I submit in all confidence that generally speaking he will find that those who live on a higher standard are more efficient; and that equalizes the difference in the standard of living.
With regard to the point raised by the hon. member for North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm) as to the wages being paid to workmen in Canadian mills, I submit to him and to the House that we must take into account, not the nominal wages, but the real wages the workmen receive; that is to say, the purchasing power of the money which they receive in this country as compared with the purchasing power of the money which the workmen receive in Great Britain, and if that is taken into consideration I think we shall find that the two sets of workmen are practically on a par. In that connection I would like to submit to the same hon. member and to the House that it is in the interest of the manufacturers that the cost of living, which is enhanced in this country by tariff duties, should be reduced. That will make the production of manufactured goods cheaper, and will not only enable our own people to get these goods cheaper but will also enable our manufacturers to compete to some extent in the foreign market.
With regard to the whole situation it seems to me that we ought to have some kind of fundamental principle to which to refer our specific acts. If we are going to adopt the principle and policy that every particular industry has got to be made to pay, and if we are going to subsidize them by state action until they do pay, then the only thing to do is to have a fair deal all round. The farmers sky, and I think they could prove with absolute certainty, that under present conditions they cannot produce wheat, particularly in our western provinces, and make ends meet. If we are going to follow the policy with regard to them that we have followed in the case of some of the manufacturers, we shall have to give them a subsidy or bounty on their wheat. I think a farmer could make a nice little profit with a bounty of 50 cents a bushel on his wheat. If we are going to adopt the principle, make it fair all round. But I submit that the whole thing is unsound, and if we are going to follow that principle we shall get led into all kinds of difficulties. I would like to see this government, as I have stated on previous occasions recognize that there are a lot of industries like people walking on stilts. They have to be got down to the ground, and they should be got down as quickly as possible, and then we shall have a condition where industries that are natural to this country will be developed, and industries that cannot be made to pay in- this country will not be maintained as parasites on the successful and indigenous industries. I think there has been, and is now, a good deal of fallacy in regard to a number of these questions.
Just one other point before I sit down. The hon. ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Dray-stated that in his opinion domestic competition would regulate prices, and therefore we did not need to take account of the tariff. I submit that under the protection of the tariff it is almost inevitable in a great variety of industries that manufacturers should get together and agree on prices, and pretty soon we have no competition. If we could maintain real active competition among the manufacturers, then the protective duty would not be so serious, but the fact of the matter is the tariff is an encouragement to combines, and pretty soon we are up against the situation where there is not any competition and the consumers are exploited for the benefit of a monopoly. If we could preserve competition it would not be so very serious a matter, because all profits tend to the same level, but where you have no real competition, and I do think that in many, many lines we have had no real competition at all, it is a very serious matter to maintain the tariff.

It seems to me that these businesses are being injured to a considerable extent by this British preference, and it does strike me that it would not make much difference, if I were a manufacturer of this particular line of goods, whether I was hurt by my own relatives overseas or was put out of business by other means. If I am to be put out of business at all, I cannot see that it makes a great deal of difference whether it is done by Englishmen or by Frenchmen. No doubt there is a certain degree of sentiment in the former case; some hon. gentlemen might say-perhaps, that it would be preferable to be put [DOT]out of business by the English people.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Excise
speechtext: Suppose I said that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This item must be considered in relation to the object we have in view. We have been anxious to cultivate trade relations with Australia; I think we all agree to that. The late government had been in negotiation with Australia with a view to coming to some understanding if possible in this matter. They laboured in all sincerity.
but I do not think they were very successful. We have now taken the matter up and are trying to come to some arrangement with the Australian authorities. If we agree that it is desirable to make some arrangement with Australia in order that we may have access to their markets for our own products, we must be prepared to meet them in some way by making some concession. We have offered them our British preference in return for the preference they give to Great Britain, but so far they have not been willing to accept this proposal. There is a hitch for the moment, but it has been intimated to us, not only by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) who has personal knowledge of the matter, but also by others interested in the Australian business, that if we make this concession in regard to the duty on raisins and currants it will go a long way towards disposing the Australians to come to terms with us. If they are pleased to take that view, foolish though it may seem to some people, and small though the point may be, we think it is worth our while, in view of the consideration that such a concession as this may influence the Australian policy in our favour, to do what is now proposed if the sacirfice is not too great. That is the whole story. Unquestionably we want to do business with them, but so far we have not been able to. This is proposed as one way of bringing about an understanding that will be beneficial to us, and I ask the House to agree to it on that ground. In the meantime, for the reason I have stated, some months will elapse before we shall do business with them and the duty will not be imposed immediately. If they meet us in the proper spirit and concede something which we consider will benefit the whole of Canada, the question is, is this a price we can afford to pay? We think it is worth considering.
I commend the minister for coming to the conclusion that the next time he undertakes to trade he will see that he has something to trade with.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am going to get armed this time and see what the effect will be on those people who find fault.

I am not finding fault at all. When you are trying to trade on behalf of the country as a whole with another country it is a very good thing to have something to trade with, and I congratulate my hon. friend. How this particular item works out one way or the other I do not know, but I entirely agree with the principle that he should have something to

trade with, and I only regret that my hon. friend did not find that out sooner. Before adjournment at six o'clock I was saying something about what I understood my hon. friend's intention to be that, having regard to the French treaty, the relative equality between England and France was to be maintained. I would ask him to be sure that his figures are correct in respect to brandies. He will remember that he told us that cognac and armagnac are the expensive brandies and would not interfere very much in our market with Scotch and Canadian whiskies. The information I have is that having regard to the currency as well as the cost of production, the distillery cost of the cognac brandy is $3 as against $7 for Scotch whiskey and $6 for Canadian whiskey. Of course, the excise duty on the Scotch whiskey remains at $10, while the cognac brandies would take the same excise duty as our own product, namely, $9. I am further told that the cost of laying these commodities down in bulk, including distillery cost, duty, sales tax and freight, would be $19.25 for the Scotch, $16 for the Canadian, and $13.10 for the brandy. If they were bottled getting down to the usual basis of a case of twelve bottles at 1| proof spirits, the cost would be $30.88 for the Scotch, $26 for the Canadian, and $21.65 for the brandy. Of course, after having told my friend about other figures, I hesitate to say that any are correct, but this is the best information that I have and I hope he will check the information he has with a view of seeing if his former statement is correct, for I imagine he desires to leave these commodities on a parity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Although the matter has been disposed of, I am glad my hon. friend has called attention to it. I think we had better see what the competition of cognac brandy amounts to. Cognac is a common expression, but I think the cognac contemplated by the treaty is not the same article. Indeed, that was one of the points the French government attached very much importance to. They thought that a great deal of so-called cognac was not cognac brandy at all, and they did not desire a special concession for it, but they wanted to be guaranteed a fair rate for this particular cognac, which must be certified by government officials and be accompanied by their certificates. I think when that test is applied very much of the brandy my hon. friend refers to will be found not to come within the description at all. However, the information, some of which has come to me also, is rather conflicting. As the French treaty will not go into effect for some months 
I think we can safely let this remain for the time being and if from experience it be found that the French brandy gets any advantage over our Canadian spirits I would be prepared to give the matter consideration when this is in evidence.
I do not see the connection between raisins and French brandies, unless the raisins are used for home brew.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is none.

At the same time I do feel that this is rather a weak argument to put forward in favour of a preference to Australia. Raisins have become a very essential food in the ordinary family budget, and by the time this tariff reaches the consumer it will certainly mean between four and five cents a pound extra. When we have a better product in close proximity, it seems to me a little too expensive to bring raisins all the way from Australia with a view to effecting a trade agreement which may or may not be consummated for years to come. I am glad though that the resolution is to be deferred by order in council until this agreement materializes.

I understood the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) to give a list of tariffs- /imposed by other countries against the importation of raisins running all the way from 2} up to as high as 7 cents a pound. Is there any other country that gives Australia as good a market to-day as Canada in regard to a tariff duty on raisins?

We have some reason to hope that the item suggested here will be an attraction to them and will remove some of the objections they have urged and result in a more acceptable arrangement.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Because it is not. I do not believe in it at all. I do not think we get anywhere by any extensive reciprocity agreement with them. But when the minister says, "It is all right in these articles and all wrong in coal," he declares to the House that the principle he has been arguing for all these years is really nothing but air.

I should like to remove
from the minds of hon. members a misconception with reference to the duty on coal. We in the Maritime provinces are getting rather tired having people continually throwing at us that all we desire is this wonderful duty on coal. What is the duty on coal, Mr. Chairman?
A bagatelle.
A Martell.
Oh, Oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

When the duty was put on
coal some years ago it was made specific, and when it was fixed at 53 cents a ton, coal was worth about 82.25 a ton. To-day coal is worth over $5, and the duty instead of increasing, as it would have had it been ad valorem, remains the same. The result is that this wonderful duty we are supposed to be so anxious about in Nova

Scotia is to-day a 10 per cent duty. That is the protection that our Nova Scotia coal gets. That is, if the law were enforced as was intended by those who enacted it. But what are the facts?

It does not protect us
at all.

The importer buys his coal at the United States colliery as run of mine, and has it screened there so that it is divided into screened and slack coal. This is brought into Canada and he pays a duty of 53 cents a ton on the screened and 15 cents a ton on the slack coal, with the result, as I am credibly informed, that to-day this imported coal is paying an average duty of less than 35 cents a ton, or about 7i per cent ad valorem. Now, does my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni or any other gentleman on the other side of the House consider that a 7i per cent duty is a protective tariff? It is not even equivalent to a tariff for revenue. In fact it is not even half of a tariff for revenue, as we generally understand that phrase.
Let me call attention to one other thing. During the last three years of the right hon. gentleman's administration there was brought into this country from the United States over half a billion dollars' worth of coal, and the average loss in exchange during that time was about 8 per cent. Multiply $500,000,000 by 8 and you have a loss to this country of $40,000,000. It might as well have been thrown into the sea; yet no one seemed at that time to be very much alarmed or to be considering seriously the development of our own coal resources.
Personally I am fully convinced that there should be a duty on anthracite coal. If we are going to tax the poor man's coal, even at 7i per cent, why should we allow the rich man's coal to come into this country free? As a revenue producer nothing could be better than a tax upon anthracite coal. I consider therefore, that it should be advocated not only to encourage the buying of our own coal but to give us a substantial revenue. Our coal has been proved to be equal to anthracite so far as domestic needs are concerned. This has been proved beyond a doubt in the committees of this House within the last few weeks. I say we should collect a revenue on imported anthracite coal; for in doing so we collect it from the people who can afford to pay, those who are well off or comfortably off. But let us have the last of this talk of protection on Nova Scotia or New Brunswick coal when we are only collecting a duty of 7i per cent on American coal.

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff

It is very evident that the coal producers of Nova Scotia must be in a very prosperous condition when we find the hon. members for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) and Hants (Mr. Martell) disparaging the duty as small and saying that 53 cents a ton is a mere bagatelle. I trust they will join with me in suggesting that it be taken off for the benefit of British Columbia. I assure these hon. gentlemen that British Columbia would receive that bounty with the deepest gratitude; they would not look a gift horse in the mouth and say, "This is only 53 cents." I say we would be only too glad to have it; we would regard 53 cents as a substantial assistance and would be pleased indeed to receive what these hon. gentlemen do not seem to appreciate very highly.

Will my hon. friend permit me a question? We have no coal in the county of Hants; there may be coal lying dormant there, but we have not any coal mines. The hon. member for Hants is as far as possible, theoretically at least, a tariff for revenue man only. I am not advocating a tariff for the protection of any industry, but we hear too much about this question of protection for the coal industry in Nova Scotia. Nova Scotia, prior to confederation, was able to run all her affairs with about 7i per cent duty. To-day the only thing you can point to that we have any protection on at all is coal, and it is very little protection we get on it. The hon. member for Cumberland may have coal in his constituency; if he has, he has as much right to protection as any other industry in Canada, and 50 cents on a ton of coal in Nova Scotia is not half as much protection as other industries are getting in this country which are making the people of Nova Scotia hewers of wood and drawers of water. My hon. friend (Mr. Neill) is very frank when he says he wants protection; I believe he would admit himself that he is a protectionist. Comox-Albemi has no coal, therefore he is not very much concerned about protection; if Comox-Alberni had coal he would be preaching protection. There is a small duty on coal in Nova Scotia. The people of that province are prepared to accept free trade in everything; we are prepared to take the duties off coal so long as you take them off everything else.

Mr. Chairman, the hon.
gentleman said he would like to ask me a question; would he mind stating it? If he does not wish to do so, I do not desire to take up the time of the committee but I
really must repudiate the suggestion that there is no coal in Comox-Albemi. I think it is a slander on the representation I have given to that district in the House in the last two years when I am told at the end of my days that there is no coal in Comax-Alberni 1

I would like to add a word, not particularly about coal but in relation to the sentiments expressed on the question of reciprocity. When the Minister of Finance rose to reply to some suggestions that have been made, he stated that it was not right to single out one item. Well, so far as reciprocity is concerned one does not need to confine himself to one item, having regard to the present attitude of the American people.
I would recall the minister's attention to the fact that boots and shoes, which everybody in Canada must use, are allowed to enter the United States free of duty. When the minister was compiling the list here it might have occurred to him or to the government to have included boots and shoes, because that would have materially affected the carrying out of the principle of reciprocity concerning which the minister seems to be so anxious. Likewise, agricultural implements may enter the United States free of duty, and we might mention quite a number of other things in connection with which the American Congress has gone on record as making a standing offer of reciprocity. I contend that in good faith we might accept this half loaf or quarter loaf offered us at the present time by the United States government. If we are really desirous of promoting the spirit of reciprocity we have a splendid opportunity to do so now, in a measure at least. There are undoubtedly other items which could form the basis of a reciprocal agreement with the United States when the time comes, but I repeat that we might well take advantage of the opportunity now offered by the American government in the legislation at present on their statute book.

subtopic: COMBINES, MONOPOLIES, TRUSTS AND MERGERS CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Right Hon: W. L. MACKENZIE KING
(Prime Minister) moved the second reading of and concurrence in an amendment made by the Senate to Bill No. 54 to provide for the investigation of combines, monopolies, trusts and mergers.
He said:	There is a slight amendment
offered by the Senate to the bill. It simply adds that the statement which must be submitted when the six applicants make application for an investigation shall be in the form of a solemn or statutory declaration. The amendment is acceptable to the government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: COMBINES, MONOPOLIES, TRUSTS AND MERGERS CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is that the only amendment ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: COMBINES, MONOPOLIES, TRUSTS AND MERGERS CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Yes.
Motion agreed to; amendment read the second time and concurred in.
